question_html:
Suppose that you are a door-to-door salesman, selling the latest innovation in vacuum cleaners to less-than-enthusiastic customers. Today, you are planning on selling to some of the \(n\) houses along a particular street. You are a master salesman, so for each house, you have already worked out the amount \(c_i\) of profit that you will make from the person in house \(i\) if you talk to them. Unfortunately, you cannot sell to every house, since if a person's neighbour sees you selling to them, they will hide and not answer the door for you. Therefore, you must select a subset of houses to sell to such that none of them are next to each other, and such that you make the maximum amount of money.

For example, if there are 10 houses and the profits that you can make from each of them are 50, 10, 12, 65, 40, 95, 100, 12, 20, 30, then it is optimal to sell to the houses 1, 4, 6, 8, 10 for a total profit of $252. Devise a dynamic programming algorithm to solve this problem, i.e. to return the maximum profit you can obtain.

  • (a) Describe in plain English, the optimal substructure present in the problem.
  • (b) Define a set of overlapping subproblems that are based on the optimal substructure.
  • (c) What are the base case subproblems and what are their values?
  • (d) Write a recurrence relation that describes the solutions to the subproblems.
  • (e) Write pseudocode that implements all of this as a dynamic programming algorithm.
  • (f) Extend your solution so that it returns an optimal subset of houses to sell to, in addition to the maximum possible profit.
solution_html:
(a) Let the houses on the street be numbered from 1 to \(n\) from left to right. The constraint that we cannot sell to the neighbours of a house is equivalent to the constraint that if we sell to house \(i\), then we cannot sell to house \(i-1\). If we do decide to sell to house \(i\), then we cannot have sold anything to house \(i-1\), but we are allowed to sell to a valid subset of houses from 1 to \(i-2\). If we do not decide to sell to house \(i\), then any valid subset of houses from 1 to \(i-1\) is acceptable to sell to.

The optimal substructure: if house \(i\) is the last house we consider selling to, and we chose to sell to it, then we cannot sell to house \(i-1\) and must make maximum profit from houses \([1..i-2]\). If we decide not to sell to house \(i\), we must sell to houses \([1..i-1]\) to make maximum profit.

(b) Define subproblems as: \(\text{DP}[i] = \{\text{the maximum profit that we can make from selling to a subset of the houses } [1..i]\}\), for all \(1 \leq i \leq n\).

(c) When there is just a single house, we should sell to it, so \(\text{DP}[1] = c_1\). When there are no houses, no profit can be made, so \(\text{DP}[0] = 0\).

(d) Recurrence relation:

\[\text{DP}[i] = \begin{cases} \max(\text{DP}[i-1],\, \text{DP}[i-2] + c_i) & i > 1 \\ c_i & i = 1 \\ 0 & i = 0 \end{cases}\]

The maximum represents the choice of either deciding not to sell to house \(i\) or deciding to sell to house \(i\). The optimal solution to the problem is the value of \(\text{DP}[n]\).

(e) A bottom-up implementation:

function SALESMAN(c[1..n])
    Set DP[0..n] = 0
    DP[1] = c_1
    for i = 1 to n do
        DP[i] = max(DP[i-1], DP[i-2] + c_i)
    return DP[n]

(f) To reconstruct the optimal set of houses, observe that house \(i\) is optimal to sell to if \(\text{DP}[i] > \text{DP}[i-1]\). A simple backtracking procedure:

function SALESMAN(c[1..n])
    Set DP[0..n] = 0
    DP[1] = c_1
    for i = 1 to n do
        DP[i] = max(DP[i-1], DP[i-2] + c_i)
    Set houses = []
    Set i = n
    while i > 0 do
        if DP[i] > DP[i-1] then
            houses.append(i)
            i = i - 2
        else
            i = i - 1
    return DP[n], houses

We subtract 2 from \(i\) if we decide to include house \(i\), so that we cannot accidentally sell to house \(i-1\) as well; otherwise we subtract 1.

question_html:
You find yourself curiously stranded on an \(n \times n\) grid, unsure of how you got there, or how to leave. Some of the cells of the grid are blocked and cannot be walked through. You are currently standing at the bottom-left corner of the grid, and are only able to move up (to the next row) and to the right (to the next column). How many ways can you walk to the top-right corner of the grid while avoiding blocked cells? You may assume that the bottom-left and top-right cells are not blocked. For example, in a sample grid, the answer is 19.

Write a dynamic programming algorithm that, given a grid as input, counts the number of valid paths from the bottom-left cell to the top-right cell. Your algorithm should run in \(O(n^2)\) time.
solution_html:
Denote the bottom-left corner as cell \((1,1)\) and the top-right corner as cell \((n,n)\). Standing in cell \((i,j)\), you have two choices: move to cell \((i+1,j)\) or to cell \((i,j+1)\).

Define subproblems: \(\text{DP}[i,j] = \{\text{The number of valid paths from cell } (i,j) \text{ to cell } (n,n)\}\), for all \(1 \leq i,j \leq n\).

Recurrence:

\[\text{DP}[i,j] = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } (i,j) = (n,n) \\ 0 & \text{if } (i,j) \text{ is blocked} \\ \text{DP}[i, j+1] & \text{if } i = n \\ \text{DP}[i+1, j] & \text{if } j = n \\ \text{DP}[i+1,j] + \text{DP}[i,j+1] & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]

The value \(\text{DP}[1,1]\) is the solution. There are a total of \(n^2\) subproblems, and each of them can be evaluated in constant time, hence the time complexity is \(O(n^2)\).

Alternatively, you can solve it using the symmetrical subproblems \(\text{DP}'[i,j] = \{\text{The number of valid paths from cell } (1,1) \text{ to cell } (i,j)\}\), solving for \(\text{DP}'[n,n]\).

question_html:
You find yourself on yet another \(n \times n\) grid, but this time, it is more exciting. Each cell of the grid has a certain non-negative amount of money on it! Denote the amount of money in the cell of row \(i\), column \(j\) by \(c_{i,j}\). You are standing on the bottom-left corner \((1,1)\) of the grid. From any cell, you can only move up (to the next row) or right (to the next column). What is the maximum amount of money that you can collect?

Given \(c_{i,j}\) for every cell, describe a dynamic programming algorithm to solve this problem. Your algorithm should run in \(O(n^2)\) time.
solution_html:
This problem is very similar to Problem 2. Standing in cell \((i,j)\), we have two choices: move up to cell \((i+1,j)\) or move right to cell \((i,j+1)\). We should select the best of the two, whichever leads to a greater amount of money.

Define subproblems: \(\text{DP}[i,j] = \{\text{The maximum amount of money we can make starting from cell } (i,j)\}\).

Recurrence:

\[\text{DP}[i,j] = c_{i,j} + \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } (i,j) = (n,n) \\ \text{DP}[i+1,j] & \text{if } j = n \\ \text{DP}[i,j+1] & \text{if } i = n \\ \max(\text{DP}[i,j+1],\, \text{DP}[i+1,j]) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]

The optimal solution is the value of \(\text{DP}[1,1]\). There are \(n^2\) subproblems, and each takes constant time to solve, so the solution takes \(O(n^2)\) time.

question_html:
Consider a sequence \(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n\) of length \(n\). A subsequence of a sequence \(a\) is any sequence that can be obtained by only deleting elements of \(a\). Devise a dynamic programming algorithm that finds the length of a longest increasing subsequence of \(a\). That is, a longest possible subsequence that consists of elements in strictly increasing order. Your algorithm should run in \(O(n^2)\) time.

For example, given the sequence \(\{0, 8, 4, 12, 2, 10, 6, 14, 1, 9, 5, 13, 3, \mathbf{11}, \mathbf{7}, \mathbf{15}\}\), the longest increasing subsequence is \(\{0, 2, 6, 9, 11, 15\}\) of length 6.
solution_html:
Consider a particular sequence \(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n\) and a longest increasing subsequence of it, say \(a_{j_1}, a_{j_2}, \ldots, a_{j_k}\). The key observation is that of all increasing subsequences of \(a\) that end with the element at position \(j_{k-1}\), this one is the longest. If it were not, we could replace the prefix of our proposed longest increasing subsequence with a longer one.

This suggests the following subproblems for a dynamic programming approach:

\(\text{DP}[i] = \{\text{The length of the longest increasing subsequence that ends with the element at position } i\}\), for \(1 \leq i \leq n\).

To find the longest increasing subsequence that ends with the element at position \(i\), we need to figure out what its prefix could have been. The prefix could be any subsequence that ends with an element \(a[j]\) such that \(a[j] < a[i]\). So, we try all of the preceding elements and pick the best one:

\[\text{DP}[i] = 1 + \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } a[i] \leq a[j] \text{ for all } j < i, \\ \displaystyle\max_{\substack{1 \leq j < i \\ a[j] < a[i]}} \text{DP}[j] & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}\]

The solution is then the maximum value of \(\text{DP}[i]\) (note: the solution is not necessarily the value of \(\text{DP}[n]\), since the longest increasing subsequence might not include the element \(a_n\)). There are \(n\) subproblems, each of which takes \(O(n)\) time to evaluate, hence the solution takes \(O(n^2)\) time.

question_html: Consider a pair of sequences \(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n\) and \(b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_m\) of length \(n\) and \(m\). Devise a dynamic programming algorithm that finds the length of a longest common subsequence of \(a\) and \(b\). A common subsequence is a sequence that is both a subsequence of \(a\) and a subsequence of \(b\). Your algorithm should run in \(O(nm)\) time. [Hint: This problem is very similar to the edit distance problem.]
solution_html:
Consider two sequences \((a_i)_{1 \leq i \leq n}\) and \((b_i)_{1 \leq i \leq m}\) and a longest common subsequence of the two \((c_i)_{1 \leq i \leq k}\). Suppose that the final element in the longest common subsequence \(c_k\) occurs at position \(i_1\) in \(a\), and at position \(i_2\) in \(b\). The remaining prefix of \(c\) must be a longest common subsequence of \(a[1..i_1-1]\) and \(b[1..i_2-1]\). This suggests that our subproblems should involve the prefixes of the sequences \(a\) and \(b\).

Define subproblems: \(\text{DP}[i,j] = \{\text{The length of a longest common subsequence of } a[1..i] \text{ and } b[1..j]\}\), for all \(0 \leq i \leq n,\, 0 \leq j \leq m\).

To write the recurrence: if the prefixes \(a[1..i]\) and \(b[1..j]\) end in the same element (i.e. \(a[i] = b[j]\)), then that element is the final element of a longest common subsequence of \(a[1..i]\) and \(b[1..j]\). If they differ, we simply try removing either \(a[i]\) or \(b[j]\):

\[\text{DP}[i,j] = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } i = 0 \text{ or } j = 0 \\ 1 + \text{DP}[i-1, j-1] & \text{if } a[i] = b[j] \\ \max(\text{DP}[i-1, j],\, \text{DP}[i, j-1]) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]

The solution is the value of \(\text{DP}[n, m]\). There are \(O(nm)\) subproblems, and each of them can be evaluated in constant time, hence this solution runs in \(O(nm)\) time.

question_html:
(Part b of Problem 5) Consider a sequence of integers \(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n\) of length \(n\). Devise a dynamic programming algorithm that finds the subarray of \(a\) with maximum sum. A subarray or substring of \(a\) is a contiguous subsequence, i.e. a subsequence consisting of consecutive elements.

  • (a) Your algorithm should run in \(O(n^2)\) time.
  • (b) Your algorithm should run in \(O(n)\) time. [Hint: Be greedy]
solution_html:
\(O(n^2)\) solution: We compute the sums \(a[i..j]\) for all substrings \([i..j]\). Doing so naively would take \(O(n^3)\) time, but since \(\text{sum}(a[i..j]) = \text{sum}(a[1..j]) - \text{sum}(a[1..i-1])\), we can use dynamic programming to compute them all in \(O(n^2)\) time. We write the subproblems:

\(\text{DP}[i] = \{\text{The sum of the elements in } a[1..i]\}\), for \(0 \leq i \leq n\).

\[\text{DP}[i] = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } i = 0 \\ \text{DP}[i-1] + a_i & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]

The solution is the maximum value of \(\text{DP}[j] - \text{DP}[i]\) for \(0 \leq i \leq j \leq n\). We have \(O(n)\) subproblems each taking constant time, then spend \(O(n^2)\) time trying all intervals \([i..j]\), giving total time \(O(n^2)\).

\(O(n)\) solution (Kadane's algorithm): We use the observation that if the sum in the interval \(a[i..j]\) is positive, it is better to extend that sum using element \(j+1\) than to start a new sum. Define \(\text{DP}'[0] = 0\) and for \(1 \leq j \leq n\):

\(\text{DP}'[j] = \displaystyle\max_{1 \leq i \leq j} \sum_{k=i}^{j} a_k\)

\[\text{DP}'[j] = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } j = 0 \\ \text{DP}'[j-1] + a_j & \text{if } \text{DP}'[j-1] > 0 \\ a_j & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]

The solution is the maximum value of \(\text{DP}'[j]\) over all \(j\). There are \(O(n)\) subproblems each evaluatable in constant time, hence the solution runs in \(O(n)\) time. Since each subproblem only cares about the previous subproblem, we can apply the space-saving trick and solve the problem in \(O(1)\) auxiliary space.

question_html:
Consider a sequence of integers \(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n\) of length \(n\). Devise a dynamic programming algorithm that finds the subarray of \(a\) with maximum sum. A subarray or substring of \(a\) is a contiguous subsequence, i.e. a subsequence consisting of consecutive elements.

  • (a) Your algorithm should run in \(O(n^2)\) time.
  • (b) Your algorithm should run in \(O(n)\) time. [Hint: Be greedy]
solution_html:
\(O(n^2)\) solution: We compute the sums \(a[i..j]\) for all substrings \([i..j]\). Since \(\text{sum}(a[i..j]) = \text{sum}(a[1..j]) - \text{sum}(a[1..i-1])\), we use DP:

\(\text{DP}[i] = \{\text{The sum of the elements in } a[1..i]\}\), for \(0 \leq i \leq n\).

\[\text{DP}[i] = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } i = 0 \\ \text{DP}[i-1] + a_i & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]

The solution is the maximum value of \(\text{DP}[j] - \text{DP}[i]\) for \(0 \leq i \leq j \leq n\). Total time: \(O(n^2)\).

\(O(n)\) solution (Kadane's algorithm): If the sum in interval \(a[i..j]\) is positive, it is better to extend that sum using element \(j+1\). Let \(\text{DP}'[0] = 0\) and for \(1 \leq j \leq n\):

\[\text{DP}'[j] = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } j = 0 \\ \text{DP}'[j-1] + a_j & \text{if } \text{DP}'[j-1] > 0 \\ a_j & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]

The solution is the maximum value of \(\text{DP}'[j]\) over all \(j\). There are \(O(n)\) subproblems, each evaluatable in constant time, giving \(O(n)\) total. Can be solved in \(O(1)\) auxiliary space by keeping only the maximum seen so far.

question_html:
You are a young child, out for a walk with your parent. You are walking down a quiet street. Your parent is in a hurry, but you are more interested in collecting pretty rocks. Your parent has agreed to a compromise where they are happy for you to cross the street back and forth to pick up rocks, but only if you keep up.

Since you are a very organised child, you have determined the value to you of each rock along both sides of the streets, and represented this data in 2 arrays, left and right, of equal length. The \(i^{th}\) element in an array represents the value of the rock on the \(i^{th}\) square of pavement on that side of the street.

Because of your parent's rule about keeping up, if you are on pavement square \(i\) on one side of the street you can either:

  • Pick up the rock on square \(i\) on that side, and move to square \(i+1\) on the same side.
  • Cross the street diagonally to square \(i+1\) on the other side (but not pick up the rock).

You start on pavement 0 on the left side of the street.

Devise a dynamic programming algorithm to determine the maximum value of rocks that you can obtain. Your algorithm should run in \(O(n)\), where \(n\) is the length of left.
solution_html:
Since the street has 2 sides, and which side we are on affects our options, we need to keep track of this. Define two arrays, DPleft and DPright, with the following overlapping subproblems:

  • \(\text{DPleft}[i] = \{\text{The maximum value we can obtain if we started from pavement } i \text{ on the left}\}\)
  • \(\text{DPright}[i] = \{\text{The maximum value we can obtain if we started from pavement } i \text{ on the right}\}\)

The last cell in each array is just the value of the rock on that square of pavement. For any other cell, the value is the maximum of picking up the rock and moving one cell along, or not picking up the rock and crossing the road.

\[\text{DPleft}[i] = \begin{cases} \text{left}[n] & \text{if } i = n \\ \max(\text{left}[i] + \text{DPleft}[i+1],\; \text{DPright}[i+1]) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]\[\text{DPright}[i] = \begin{cases} \text{right}[n] & \text{if } i = n \\ \max(\text{right}[i] + \text{DPright}[i+1],\; \text{DPleft}[i+1]) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]

The answer is \(\text{DPleft}[0]\) (since we start on pavement 0 on the left side).

question_html:
A ferry that is going to carry cars across the bay has two lanes of length \(L\) in which cars can drive onto. The \(n\) cars that wish to board the ferry line up in a single lane, and are individually directed onto one of the two lanes of the ferry until the next car cannot fit in either lane. Depending on which lanes the cars are directed onto, fewer or more cars may fit on the ferry. Let \(\ell_i\) denote the length of car \(i\) and assume that:

  • \(L\) is a positive integer.
  • Each \(\ell_i\) is a positive integer between 1 and \(L\).
  • The distance between cars when packed into the ship is negligible.

Write a dynamic programming solution that determines the maximum number of cars that can be loaded onto the ferry if distributed optimally.

  • (a) Solve the problem in whatever time complexity you can (without resorting to brute force).
  • (b) Improve your solution to \(O(nL)\) time complexity (if it is not already).

For example, suppose that the car lengths are 2, 2, 7, 4, 9, 8, 1, 7, 3, 3 and the ferry is 20 units long. An optimal solution is to load 8 cars in lanes arranged like 2, 2, 7, 9 and 4, 8, 1, 7.
solution_html:
We are looking for the longest prefix of \(\ell_1, \ell_2, \ldots, \ell_n\) that we can fit onto the ferry without going over the lanes' length limit \(L\). This is similar to knapsack — we have two lanes (two knapsacks).

Part (a) — \(O(nL^2)\) solution:

Define subproblems: \(\text{DP}[i, L_1, L_2] = \{\text{The maximum number of cars from car } i \text{ onwards that can be loaded onto the ship with } L_1 \text{ room left in the first lane and } L_2 \text{ room left in the second lane}\}\), for all \(1 \leq i \leq n+1\) and \(0 \leq L_1, L_2 \leq L\).

\[\text{DP}[i,L_1,L_2] = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } i = n+1 \\ 0 & \text{if } \ell_i > L_1 \text{ and } \ell_i > L_2 \\ 1 + \text{DP}[i+1, L_1 - \ell_i, L_2] & \text{if } \ell_i \leq L_1 \text{ and } \ell_i > L_2 \\ 1 + \text{DP}[i+1, L_1, L_2 - \ell_i] & \text{if } \ell_i > L_1 \text{ and } \ell_i \leq L_2 \\ 1 + \max(\text{DP}[i+1, L_1-\ell_i, L_2],\, \text{DP}[i+1, L_1, L_2-\ell_i]) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]

This solution has \(O(nL^2)\) subproblems.

Part (b) — \(O(nL)\) solution:

We can optimise by noting that if we have loaded cars 1 to \(i\), their total weight is \(\sum_{j=1}^{i} \ell_j\). This means \((L - L_1) + (L - L_2) = \sum_{j=1}^{i} \ell_j\), so \(L_2\) is determined by \(L_1\). Reduce to one parameter:

\(\text{DP}[i, L_1] = \{\text{The maximum number of cars from car } i \text{ onwards that can be loaded onto the ship with } L_1 \text{ room left in the first lane}\}\), for \(1 \leq i \leq n+1\) and \(0 \leq L_1 \leq L\). Compute \(L_2 = 2L - L_1 - \sum_{j=1}^{i-1} \ell_j\) on the fly using precomputed prefix sums.

\[\text{DP}[i,L_1] = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } i = n+1 \\ 0 & \text{if } \ell_i > L_1 \text{ and } \ell_i > 2L - L_1 - \sum_{j=1}^{i-1}\ell_j \\ 1 + \text{DP}[i+1, L_1 - \ell_i] & \text{if } \ell_i \leq L_1 \text{ and } \ell_i > 2L - L_1 - \sum_{j=1}^{i-1}\ell_j \\ 1 + \text{DP}[i+1, L_1] & \text{if } \ell_i > L_1 \text{ and } \ell_i \leq 2L - L_1 - \sum_{j=1}^{i-1}\ell_j \\ 1 + \max(\text{DP}[i+1, L_1-\ell_i],\, \text{DP}[i-1, L_1]) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]

The answer is the value of \(\text{DP}[1, L]\). This solution has \(\Theta(nL)\) subproblems, each evaluatable in constant time, hence it runs in \(\Theta(nL)\) time.

question_html:
You and your friend are going to play a game. You start with a row of \(n\) coins with values \(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n\). You will each take turns to remove either the first or last coin. You continue until there are no coins left, and your score is the total value of the coins that you removed. You will make the first move of the game.

  • (a) Show that the greedy strategy in which you simply pick the most valuable coin every time is not optimal.
  • (b) Devise a dynamic programming algorithm that determines the maximum possible score that you can achieve if both you and your friend make the best possible moves.

For example, given the coins 6, 9, 1, 2, 16, 8, the maximum value that you can achieve when going first is 23.
solution_html:
(a) The greedy strategy is not always optimal. For instance, if the sequence is 2, 100, 1, 1: if you take 2 (the larger of the two ends), your friend takes 100, and you lose. But if you take the 1 from the right, no matter what your friend takes, you get the 100 and win.

(b) At each stage of the game, the coins that remain will be some contiguous subarray of the original coins. Suppose we are currently looking at the subarray from \(i\) to \(j\) inclusive. We have exactly two choices: take element \(i\) or take element \(j\).

Define subproblems: \(\text{DP}[i,j] = \{\text{The maximum score that we can obtain playing first from the subarray } a[i..j]\}\), for \(1 \leq i \leq j \leq n\).

Base case: when \(i = j\), we have \(\text{DP}[i,j] = a_i\).

For the recurrence: if we take element \(i\), our friend will take the maximum score possible from elements \(a[i+1..j]\), so their score will be \(\text{DP}[i+1,j]\), and our score will be \(\text{sum}(a[i..j]) - \text{DP}[i+1,j]\). Similarly, if we select element \(j\), our score will be \(\text{sum}(a[i..j]) - \text{DP}[i,j-1]\). We should pick the best of the two:

\[\text{DP}[i,j] = \begin{cases} a_i & \text{if } i = j \\ \text{sum}(a[i..j]) - \min(\text{DP}[i+1,j],\, \text{DP}[i,j-1]) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]

The solution is the value of \(\text{DP}[1,n]\). This gives \(O(n^2)\) subproblems. We can evaluate each subproblem in constant time provided we can evaluate \(\text{sum}(a[i..j])\) in constant time by precomputing the partial sums. Hence we solve the problem in \(O(n^2)\) time.

question_html:
A sequence is a palindrome if it is equal to its reversal. For example, racecar and 5, 3, 2, 3, 5 are palindromes. Given a sequence \(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n\) of length \(n\), solve the following problems:

  • (a) Devise a dynamic programming algorithm that determines the length of the longest palindromic subsequence of \(a\). Your algorithm should run in \(O(n^2)\) time.
  • (b) Devise an algorithm that determines the length of the longest palindromic substring of \(a\). Your algorithm should run in \(O(n^2)\) time. (You do not have to use dynamic programming.)
  • (c) (Advanced) Devise a dynamic programming algorithm that determines the length of the longest palindromic substring of \(a\). Your algorithm should run in \(O(n)\) time.
solution_html:
(a) Longest palindromic subsequence in \(O(n^2)\):

A sequence \(a[1..n]\) is a palindrome if and only if \(a_1 = a_n\) and \(a[2..n-1]\) is also a palindrome. An empty sequence or a single element sequence are also palindromes. To build a palindromic subsequence from \(a\), we are either going to use the endpoints \(a_1\) and \(a_n\) if they are equal, or we will ignore one of them.

Define subproblems: \(\text{DP}[i,j] = \{\text{The length of the longest palindromic subsequence of } a[i..j]\}\), for all \(1 \leq i \leq j \leq n\).

\[\text{DP}[i,j] = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } i = j \\ 2 + \text{DP}[i+1, j-1] & \text{if } a[i] = a[j] \\ \max(\text{DP}[i+1, j],\, \text{DP}[i, j-1]) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]

The answer is the value of \(\text{DP}[1,n]\). There are \(O(n^2)\) subproblems, each evaluatable in constant time, hence this algorithm runs in \(O(n^2)\).

(b) Longest palindromic substring in \(O(n^2)\):

A palindrome is symmetric about the middle. One way to detect a palindrome is to try all \(O(n)\) middle points and see how wide we can make the substring before it becomes asymmetrical. We must try each element as the middle (giving odd-length palindromes) and also all gaps between elements (giving even-length palindromes). Since we try \(O(n)\) middle points and each substring can only be \(O(n)\) long, this solution takes \(O(n^2)\).

function LONGEST_PALINDROME(a[1..n])
    Set answer = 1
    for i = 1 to n do
        Set j = 1
        while i - j >= 1 and i + j <= n and a[i-j] = a[i+j] do
            answer = max(answer, 2j+1)
            j = j + 1
        Set j = 0
        while i - j + 1 >= 1 and i + j <= n and a[i-j+1] = a[i+j] do
            answer = max(answer, 2j)
            j = j + 1
    return answer

(c) Longest palindromic substring in \(O(n)\) — Manacher's algorithm:

To solve this problem in \(O(n)\) requires significantly more effort. First, we assume WLOG that we only need a solution for seeking palindromes of odd length (even-length palindromes can be handled by padding with identical separator elements between every adjacent pair).

Define: \(\text{DP}[i] = \{\text{The radius of the largest odd-length palindrome centered at position } i\}\). A palindrome of radius \(r\) is length \(2r + 1\).

We compute this DP using observations about the symmetry of palindromes. Suppose we know that at position \(i\), the radius of the largest palindrome is \(r\). For position \(j\) falling inside this radius, by symmetry at \(i\), the position \(2i - j\) (the mirror of \(j\)) gives us information about the palindrome at \(j\). If the palindrome at \(2i-j\) falls completely inside the radius at \(i\), then \(\text{DP}[j] = \text{DP}[2i-j]\). Otherwise, we can deduce \(\text{DP}[j] \geq i + r - j\) and extend naively from there. The algorithm runs in \(O(n)\) total since the current radius always moves to the right and can move at most \(n\) steps.

function LONGEST_PALINDROME(a[1..n])
    Set answer = 1
    Set DP[i] = 0 for all 1 <= i <= n
    Set i = 1, r = 0
    for j = 2 to n do
        Set w = min(DP[2i-j], i + r - j) if j < i + r else 0
        while j - w >= 1 and j + w <= n and a[j-w] = a[j+w] do
            w = w + 1
        if j + w > i + r then
            i = j, r = w
        DP[i] = w
        answer = max(answer, 2w+1)
    return answer
